name: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 28 (AFG3L2)
aliases: autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia type SCA28

clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant, early-onset and slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia caused mostly by missense variants in AFG3L2
AFG3L2 is a subunit of the mitochondrial m-AAA protease, so SCA28 is fundamentally a disorder of mitochondrial protein quality control
A distinguishing clinical clue is ophthalmoparesis, particularly limitation of upgaze, often accompanied by ptosis
Core features include gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria and nystagmus, with pyramidal signs such as hyperreflexia in many patients
Onset is frequently in childhood or early adulthood, earlier than many other dominant spinocerebellar ataxias
Diagnosis is by gene sequencing, since repeat-expansion assays are normal
Brain MRI shows cerebellar atrophy that is often vermian-predominant
Biallelic AFG3L2 variants cause a distinct severe recessive spastic ataxia and neurodevelopmental phenotype, in contrast to the dominant SCA28
reference.pathophysiology: SCA28 is caused by dominant variants in AFG3L2, which encodes a subunit of the m-AAA protease in the inner mitochondrial membrane. This protease degrades misfolded proteins and processes substrates that govern mitochondrial function and calcium handling. Pathogenic variants, often clustered in the proteolytic domain, impair protease activity and disturb mitochondrial protein homeostasis and calcium regulation. Purkinje cells are especially dependent on this quality-control system, so its failure leads to progressive Purkinje cell degeneration, producing cerebellar ataxia with the characteristic ophthalmoparesis.
additionalDifferentials: Other early-onset autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxias (SCA5, SCA14)
Mitochondrial ataxias and chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia, given the ophthalmoparesis
SPG7-related spastic ataxia, involving the partner protease subunit paraplegin
Friedreich ataxia and other early-onset ataxias
additionalInvestigations: AFG3L2 sequencing within an ataxia gene panel or exome
Brain MRI to document cerebellar (often vermian) atrophy
Testing for common repeat-expansion SCAs to exclude commoner causes
Evaluation for a mitochondrial disorder or external ophthalmoplegia given eye-movement involvement
SPG7 testing where a spastic-ataxic overlap is present
Detailed family history to establish dominant transmission
redFlags: Rapid progression or severe bulbar and respiratory involvement suggesting an alternative cause
A severe childhood presentation with marked spasticity raising the possibility of recessive AFG3L2 disease
New focal neurological signs indicating a structural lesion
Dysphagia with aspiration risk requiring swallow assessment
reference.prognosis: SCA28 is slowly progressive, and many patients retain independent walking for a prolonged period; life expectancy is often relatively preserved in the dominant form, with disability determined by cumulative cerebellar dysfunction, ophthalmoparesis and any bulbar involvement.
pitfalls: Overlooking ophthalmoparesis, a useful clue that helps distinguish SCA28 from other dominant ataxias
Expecting a repeat expansion and missing the point mutation when common panels are negative
Confusing dominant SCA28 with the distinct severe recessive AFG3L2 phenotype
Failing to consider the related SPG7 protease disorder in spastic-ataxic presentations
Not providing genetic counselling given dominant inheritance and variable expressivity
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists for this AFG3L2-related ataxia, so centre care on physiotherapy for gait and balance, occupational therapy, and speech and language therapy
Manage the ophthalmoparesis, ptosis and resulting diplopia with orthoptic assessment, prisms, and ptosis props or lid surgery where needed
Treat pyramidal spasticity with physiotherapy and an antispasticity agent such as baclofen
Institute falls prevention and provide mobility aids for gait and limb ataxia
Monitor for bulbar dysfunction with periodic swallow assessment
Offer genetic counselling and cascade testing for the autosomal dominant, often early-onset disorder
